title: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook (November 2026) — the first monthly revision to the Winter Fuels Outlook, not the Winter Fuels Outlook itself
source: EST: eia.gov/outlooks/steo/release_schedule.php, re-fetched direct 2026-09-08 (HTTP 200, 54,906 bytes) and parsed cell-by-cell by this event's own initial research, lists "11/10/2026" for the November 2026 edition with an EMPTY Notes cell. Release window stated on the same page as 12:00-12:15 pm ET. The date reproduces independently from that page's stated rule ("the first Tuesday following the first Thursday of each month", with a Federal holiday on the preceding Monday pushing the release to Wednesday): 2026-11-05 is a Thursday, the following Tuesday is 11-10, and 11-09 is not a Federal holiday (Veterans Day 2026 falls Wednesday 11-11, the day AFTER the release), so no adjustment applies. Every deviation this session could find in EIA's published history is holiday-driven, and 11-10 has no holiday interaction on either the Monday before or the release day itself. Filed estimate on two counts, neither of them date doubt: this calendar defines no `confirmed` prefix for the EIA (the standing schema gap eia-steo-2026-09-09 named), and this lane never self-confirms an event it discovered in-sweep. Checked 2026-09-08
notes: Canonical entry written by this event's own never-assessed initial research (2026-09-08), promoting the sole prior proposal eia-steo-2026-11-10.from-eia-steo-2026-10-06.json — and CORRECTING that proposal's headline claim, which is the main finding of this session. The proposal titled this "the Winter Fuels Outlook edition" and reasoned from the NG=F base rate on that basis. The Winter Fuels Outlook is an OCTOBER product, not a November one, and four independent EIA primaries say so: (1) the 2026 schedule table's Notes cell attaches "Winter Fuels Outlook" to the October 2026 row (10/06/2026), leaving November 2026 blank; (2) the 2027 table does the same for October 2027 (10/13/2027); (3) an archived banner still served inside an HTML comment on the live STEO landing page reads "We will release our Winter Fuels Outlook on Wednesday October 15" and links /outlooks/steo/report/perspectives/2025/10-winterfuels/ — the 2025 edition, an October release; (4) the 2024-25 Winter Fuels article's own forecast-comparison tables are labelled "Release date: October 8, 2024" for the outlook itself. So the October sibling eia-steo-2026-10-06 owns the Winter Fuels Outlook, and THIS edition is its first monthly revision. MEASURED this session and new to this repo — what that revision has actually been worth. EIA publishes an Oct/Nov/Dec/Jan/Feb/Mar comparison grid for each winter; across the two winters reachable (2024-25 and 2025-26), the November revision to household winter fuel expenditure runs 0.2%-4.8% (natural gas +2.7% and +2.6%, electricity +0.8% and +0.9%, propane +3.5% and -0.2%, heating oil -4.8% and +1.7%, heating degree days +2.5% and +1.3%), never flips a fuel's year-on-year sign, and in 7 of 10 series-observations moved AWAY from EIA's own final estimate — the October number was closer to the truth than the November one. The tape agrees: across both November editions (2024-11-13, 2025-11-12, both verified from EIA primaries), all 32 full-day |move| observations across 17 symbols sit inside each symbol's own p90, and 22 of 23 release-hour (12:00-13:00 ET) observations do; the single exception is MSFT on 2025-11-12 (1.26% vs a 0.52% p90) in an hour where CL=F moved 0.03%, which is idiosyncratic MSFT and not an energy-forecast mechanism. 2025-11-12 is the cleanest demonstration on the calendar of the sibling ledgers' thesis: CL=F moved 4.18% on the day and 0.03% in the release hour. THE DAY IS CROWDED AND THE STEO IS THE SMALLEST THING ON IT: 2026-11-10 also carries cpi-2026-11-10 (high, CONFIRMED, 08:30 ET), us-china-tariff-truce-expiry-2026-11-10 (high, estimate), boj-summary-of-opinions-2026-11-10, and CRWV's estimate-dated print off an 8-K cadence whose prior instance printed midday — so CRWV may share the STEO's own noon window. Attribution rule stated in advance: an energy-heavy CPI headline at 08:30 owns the day, any CRWV move is the print, and the STEO owns the noon hour alone. Filed `low` on the sibling entries' reasoning: a forecast publication sets no policy and moves no equity tape, and this calendar's names are `symbols: []` away from it.
